blocks.md: **Merge sort: splitting is trivial, ORDER is created during the MERGE. Quicksort: hard work happens during PARTITION, merging is trivial. Two opposite philosophies.**

blocks.label: merge sort — full skeleton
blocks.py:
def merge_sort(a):
    if len(a) <= 1: return a
    m = len(a) // 2
    L, R = merge_sort(a[:m]), merge_sort(a[m:])
    out, i, j = [], 0, 0
    while i < len(L) and j < len(R):
        if L[i] <= R[j]: out.append(L[i]); i += 1     # <= keeps STABILITY
        else:                out.append(R[j]); j += 1
    return out + L[i:] + R[j:]

items.title: Sort an Array (merge sort required)
items.statement: Implement merge sort from scratch (n ≤ 5×10⁴). Then justify Θ(n log n) worst case aloud.
hints: Reuse the section skeleton verbatim.
Recursion depth ~17 for 10⁵ — safe.

solutionCode.label: top-down merge sort with a reused buffer
solutionCode.py:
def sort_array(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    a = a[:]
    buf = [0] * len(a)                   # allocate ONCE, not per call

    def merge(lo, mid, hi):
        i, j, k = lo, mid, lo
        while i < mid and j < hi:
            if a[i] <= a[j]:             # <= keeps it stable
                buf[k] = a[i]; i += 1
            else:
                buf[k] = a[j]; j += 1
            k += 1
        while i < mid:
            buf[k] = a[i]; i += 1; k += 1
        while j < hi:
            buf[k] = a[j]; j += 1; k += 1
        a[lo:hi] = buf[lo:hi]

    def msort(lo, hi):
        if hi - lo < 2:                  # 0 or 1 element is already sorted
            return
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        msort(lo, mid)
        msort(mid, hi)
        if a[mid - 1] <= a[mid]:         # already ordered: skip the merge
            return
        merge(lo, mid, hi)

    msort(0, len(a))
    return a

items.complexity: Θ(n log n) in all cases — the recursion tree is always log n deep and each level merges n elements. Space O(n) for the scratch buffer.

followups.q: Justify Θ(n log n) worst case out loud.
followups.a: The array is halved every level, so the tree is log₂n deep regardless of input. Each level merges every element exactly once, costing n. Total n·log n, and because the split is positional rather than value-based, no input can unbalance it — unlike quicksort, the bound is Θ, not just O.

followups.q: Why allocate the buffer once?
followups.a: A fresh vector per merge call means O(n log n) allocations, which dominates the runtime through malloc overhead alone. One buffer reused by index range costs a single allocation. It is the difference between a textbook merge sort and one that is actually competitive.

items.title: Sort Colors (Dutch Flag)
items.statement: Sort 0s,1s,2s in ONE pass with three pointers.
hints: low=next-0 slot, high=next-2 slot, mid=scanner.
Swap mid-low advances BOTH; swap mid-high re-checks mid.

solutionCode.label: Dutch national flag: three pointers

items.complexity: One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.

followups.q: Why does mid advance on a 0-swap but not on a 2-swap?
followups.a: Everything left of `low` is already processed and can only be a 0 or 1, so the value swapped in from `low` is known-good and mid can move past it. The value swapped in from `high` comes from unexamined territory — it could be anything — so mid must re-inspect that slot.

followups.q: State the loop invariant.
followups.a: [0, low) holds 0s, [low, mid) holds 1s, (high, n) holds 2s, and [mid, high] is unexamined. The loop ends when the unexamined region is empty. Naming the four regions is what makes the three-way branch obvious rather than memorised.

items.title: Quick Sort implementation
items.statement: Full quicksort with randomized pivot; print partition index per call.
hints: rand() seeding once in main.
Verify final position invariant after each partition.

solutionCode.label: Lomuto partition with a randomised pivot
solutionCode.py:
import random


def quick_sort(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    a = a[:]

    def partition(lo, hi):
        r = random.randint(lo, hi)
        a[r], a[hi] = a[hi], a[r]        # randomised pivot parked at the end
        pivot, i = a[hi], lo - 1
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if a[j] <= pivot:
                i += 1
                a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
        a[i + 1], a[hi] = a[hi], a[i + 1]
        return i + 1                     # pivot is now in its FINAL position

    def qs(lo, hi):
        if lo >= hi:
            return
        p = partition(lo, hi)
        qs(lo, p - 1)                    # pivot excluded from both sides
        qs(p + 1, hi)

    qs(0, len(a) - 1)
    return a

items.complexity: Average O(n log n); worst case O(n²) on adversarial input, which randomising the pivot makes vanishingly unlikely. Space O(log n) for the recursion.

followups.q: What is the invariant after partition returns p?
followups.a: a[p] holds the pivot in its final sorted position — it will never move again. Everything in [lo, p) is ≤ it and everything in (p, hi] is ≥ it. That is why both recursive calls exclude p, and why quickselect can discard one side entirely.

followups.q: Why randomise, and what is left unfixed?
followups.a: A fixed last-element pivot degrades to O(n²) on sorted or reverse-sorted input — the most common real-world shape. Randomising makes any single input unlikely to be bad. It does not fix arrays of all-equal elements, where Lomuto still splits 1:n−1; three-way partitioning (S202's idea) is the cure for that.

items.title: Inversion Count
items.statement: Pairs i<j with a[i]>a[j]. Merge-sort variant counts during merging.
hints: When taking RIGHT before LEFT element, add remaining-left-count.
Use long long — inversions reach n(n−1)/2.

solutionCode.label: count crossings during the merge

items.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. The count can reach n(n−1)/2 ≈ 5×10^9 for n = 10^5, so it must be 64-bit.

followups.q: Why is `mid - i` the correct increment?
followups.a: The left half is sorted. If a[i] > a[j], then every element from i to mid−1 is also greater than a[j], because they are all ≥ a[i]. So one comparison reveals mid − i inversions at once — that batching is exactly what beats the O(n²) double loop.

followups.q: Why does `<=` matter in the comparison?
followups.a: Equal elements are not inversions. Using `<` would take from the right half on a tie and wrongly add mid − i to the count. It is also what keeps the underlying sort stable — the same character doing two jobs.

items.title: Merge Intervals
items.statement: Merge overlapping ranges. Sort-by-start converts overlap chaos into adjacent checks.
hints: Comparator: start ascending.
Overlap test: cur.start ≤ last.end.
This pattern returns in Greedy module.

solutionCode.label: sort by start, extend or append

items.complexity: O(n log n) for the sort, then one O(n) sweep. Space O(n) for the output.

followups.q: Why `max(out.back()[1], end)` rather than just `end`?
followups.a: Sorting by start says nothing about ends. [1,10] followed by [2,3] is fully contained — assigning `end` would shrink the merged interval to [1,3] and lose coverage. The max is what handles nesting.

followups.q: Why does sorting by start make one pass sufficient?
followups.a: After sorting, any interval that overlaps the current run must start before the run's end, and every later interval starts even further right. So overlap can only ever be with the most recent merged interval — you never need to look further back, which turns an all-pairs problem into a linear sweep.

items.title: Relative Sort Array
items.statement: Arrange arr1 per arr2's order first, remainder ascending — counting map does both.
hints: Count arr1; emit per arr2 order; then sweep remaining counts ascending.
Range tiny ⇒ pure counting wins over comparator gymnastics.

solutionCode.label: counting array: custom order, then ascending remainder
solutionCode.py:
def relative_sort_array(arr1: list[int], arr2: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    count = [0] * 1001                   # constraint: 0 <= values <= 1000
    for x in arr1:
        count[x] += 1
    out = []
    for x in arr2:                       # emit in arr2's order
        out.extend([x] * count[x])
        count[x] = 0
    for v in range(1001):                # leftovers, ascending
        out.extend([v] * count[v])
    return out

items.complexity: O(n + m + K) where K is the value range (1001 here). Beats O(n log n) because the range is tiny and bounded.

followups.q: Why is counting the right tool here rather than a custom comparator?
followups.a: A comparator needs a rank lookup for every comparison — O(n log n) comparisons each doing a hash probe. The value range is only 1001 wide, so a counting array answers "how many of each" in one pass and emits directly in the required order. Bounded range is the licence to skip comparison sorting entirely.

followups.q: What is the C++ `count[x]-- > 0` subtlety?
followups.a: Post-decrement tests the old value then decrements, so the loop exits with the counter at −1, not 0. Without the explicit reset, the leftover sweep would see −1 and skip correctly by luck — but a repeated value in arr2 would re-emit. Resetting makes the intent explicit rather than relying on sign.

items.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
items.statement: Most frequent chars first. Compare heap vs bucket approaches aloud.
hints: freq map then bucket[index=freq].
Bucket walk high→low = O(n); heap adds unnecessary log factor.

solutionCode.label: buckets indexed by frequency, walked high to low

items.complexity: Bucket route O(n). Heap route O(n log k) with k distinct characters. Space O(n).

followups.q: Compare the heap and bucket routes.
followups.a: A max-heap of (freq, char) costs O(k log k) to build and drain — with k ≤ 128 for ASCII that is trivially fast, and the code is shorter. Bucketing is O(n) asymptotically and avoids the log factor, but allocates an n+1 array. For bounded alphabets the heap is often the better engineering call; state that rather than reflexively optimising the exponent.

followups.q: Is the output unique?
followups.a: No. Characters with equal frequency may appear in any relative order, so "aabb" admits both "aabb" and "bbaa". Any correct test must compare frequency profiles, not exact strings — worth flagging before the interviewer writes a brittle assertion.

items.title: Largest Number
items.statement: Order integers so concatenation is maximal. Comparator a+b vs b+a as STRINGS.
hints: Compare s1+s2 > s2+s1 lexicographically.
Prove transitivity mentally — it holds (classic proof asked).
All-zeros edge: return "0" not "00…".

solutionCode.label: order by which concatenation is larger

items.complexity: O(n log n) comparisons, each costing O(d) to concatenate d-digit strings. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why compare a+b against b+a rather than comparing the numbers?
followups.a: You are choosing an order, not a magnitude. 9 beats 30 numerically and also in concatenation ("930" > "309"), but 5 versus 51 goes the other way: "551" > "515", so 5 must come first even though it is smaller. The concatenation test asks exactly the question the problem asks.

followups.q: Why is the all-zeros guard needed?
followups.a: Input [0,0] concatenates to "00", which is not a valid number representation. After sorting, a leading "0" means the largest element is 0, hence every element is — so returning "0" is both correct and the only special case required.

items.title: Height Checker
items.statement: Students out-of-line vs expected. Solve via counting array, not library sort.
hints: Heights bounded (≤100) — perfect counting territory.
Diff count between original and counting-rebuilt sequence.

solutionCode.label: counting sort, then compare positionally

items.complexity: O(n + K) with K = 101 the bounded height range. Beats O(n log n) sorting.

followups.q: Why is counting sort valid here?
followups.a: Heights are bounded to 1..100, a range independent of n. That makes an O(K) array affordable and lets you produce the sorted order without any comparisons — O(n + K) beats O(n log n) whenever K is small relative to n log n.

followups.q: Why no need to materialise the sorted array?
followups.a: The expected height at each index is generated in order by the counting sweep, so you can compare against the original as you go. Building the array first would be equally correct but costs an extra O(n) allocation for information consumed immediately.

items.title: Pancake Sorting
items.statement: Only operation = reverse prefix of length k. Sort with ≤ 2n flips.
hints: Selection idea: bring current max to front (flip to max), flip it to back.
Shrink problem size each double-flip.

solutionCode.label: selection sort by double flip: max to front, then to its place

items.complexity: At most 2n flips (2 per element), each flip O(n) — O(n²) total work. Space O(1) beyond the answer list.

followups.q: Why at most 2n flips?
followups.a: Each round places one element permanently and costs at most two flips — one to bring the maximum to the front, one to send it to the end of the unsorted region. With n rounds that is 2n, and rounds where the maximum is already in place cost zero.

followups.q: Why is only a prefix reversal allowed, and what does that force?
followups.a: It models flipping a stack of pancakes with a spatula — you can only ever invert a top segment. That rules out arbitrary swaps, so you cannot move an element without disturbing everything above it. The double-flip idiom is the standard way to relocate one element while restoring the rest.

revisionCard: Merge sort: order born in MERGE step; `<=` = stability; guaranteed n log n; Θ(n) buffer
Quicksort: order born in PARTITION; randomized pivot; worst n² anatomy = 0/(n−1) splits
Stability: stable_sort/sort difference is an interview reflex — know WHY each behaves so
Counting sort legal iff bounded key range; beats comparison lower bound by not comparing
Lower bound: any comparison sort ≥ Ω(n log n)
Inversions counted free inside merge — right-before-left event += leftover left size
Dutch flag three-way partition = duplicate-heavy quicksort fix
